Testimony in Opposition to LD 1177

Chair Teplar, Chair Doudera, and esteemed members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee:

As the Athletic Director for the Biddeford School Department, I strongly oppose LD 1177, which would impose a three-year moratorium on synthetic turf installations across Maine. This legislation undermines the principle of local control that should govern these important community decisions.

In Biddeford, our decision to install synthetic turf followed a comprehensive local evaluation process that weighed multiple factors:

 Our environmental assessment revealed that synthetic turf eliminates the need for fertilizers, herbicides, and pesticides that can leach into local waterways
 We calculated significant reductions in water usage--a growing concern as our climate changes
 We considered the carbon footprint of regular mowing and maintenance required by natural grass fields
 The safety of our student-athletes improved as our previous natural surface became dangerously hard during dry periods and excessively muddy during wet seasons
 We've seen significantly increased participation rates across all age groups, particularly among youth programs
 Weather-related cancellations have dropped dramatically, allowing for more consistent athletic programming
 Extended seasonal use has provided additional months of activity, promoting year-round physical fitness
 We've been able to host regional tournaments and events, bringing economic benefits to our community
 Our field has allowed us to assist neighboring communities during their field renovations or upgrades

While I support the committee's interest in studying environmental impacts, imposing a moratorium before completing the study could suggest a predetermined outcome. If the goal is truly to gather information, why not conduct the study without restricting local control in the meantime? This approach would respect the democratic process while still advancing our understanding of health and environmental considerations.

Additionally, as someone directly responsible for student safety, I must emphasize that this moratorium would create serious safety concerns. Fields that currently need replacement would be forced to remain in deteriorating condition for three years, potentially causing injuries to thousands of Maine students. It would be irresponsible to knowingly subject our student-athletes to these preventable risks.
It's important to recognize that these decisions are already extensively studied at the local level. Before any community moves forward with synthetic turf, thorough research and deliberation take place involving environmental experts, health professionals, and community stakeholders. Furthermore, communities have direct democratic input through public hearings, school budget votes, and construction bond approvals. This established process allows communities to make informed decisions based on the extensive studies and literature that has occurred nationwide. LD 1177 would effectively override these local voting rights and silence community voices.
Both Democrats and Republicans have historically championed local control as a cornerstone of effective governance. This principle recognizes that one-size-fits-all mandates from Augusta rarely account for the diverse needs of communities from York to Fort Kent. Local officials are directly accountable to voters and taxpayers, creating a responsive system that works best when communities retain authority over infrastructure decisions.
I respectfully urge committee members across party lines to reject this state intervention into local decision-making and instead support resources that help communities make informed, responsible choices while preserving the fundamental principle of local control.
I Thank you for your consideration.
Respectfully submitted,
Dennis Walton Athletic Director Biddeford School Department

In Support of LD 1177 Establishing a 3-year Moratorium on the Installation or Reinstallation of Synthetic Turf and Requiring a Study of the Public Health and Environmental Risks of Synthetic Turf
Committee on Environment and Natural Resources Maine Legislature, Augusta, ME April 09, 2025
Representative Gramlich, President Daughtry, and members of the Committee, thank you for reading my testimony. My name is Lillian Hyce, and I have lived in Waterville for almost 4 years as a student at Colby College. I am about to graduate this May with a BA in biology with a concentration in neuroscience and an accompanying minor in environmental science. My minor has allowed me to take many courses in public health, including Global Public Health and the Pollution and Human Health course in which I am currently enrolled this semester. I am unfortunately unavailable to deliver in-person testimony, but have taken the opportunity to submit written testimony.
I am testifying in support of LD 1177 because synthetic turf is comprised of several families of toxic chemicals harmful to human health and the environment. As a former athlete, an aunt of five children, and a once young girl who spent many hours a week on synthetic turf fields, I have personally witnessed and experienced the many routes of exposure to these chemicals through the turf. I remember having to wash my hands and body multiple times as a child after soccer practice to remove the black cast the turf would leave on my skin. If exposed wounds from athletic activity, which are quite common in my experience, come in contact with the chemicals in turf, there is a direct entry point into the bloodstream. My nieces and nephews have all attended "toddler play time" events on synthetic turf fields, unconsciously, or even consciously for small children, ingesting the small pieces of shredded tires and the green plastic blades.
I would like to focus this testimony on a specific chemical family. The presence of phthalates has been confirmed in synthetic turf. Phthalates are known endocrine disruptors that accumulate in the body. Evidence shows that maternal phthalate exposure has anti-testosterone properties on male fetuses by blocking a testosterone spike necessary for proper male fetal development, pathologically resulting in testicular dysgenesis syndrome. Additionally, phthalate exposure has various adverse health effects on women and girls, such as fertility and pregnancy problems and attention and learning disabilities, respectively.
Higher exposure in children is particularly concerning. We have a responsibility to protect and advocate for the safety of all Mainers, but especially children who do not have the health and policy literacy to understand the consequences of toxics exposure from synthetic turf. Endocrine

disruption is increasingly dangerous in fetuses, infants, and children. Proper development of the reproductive, neurological, and immunological systems in this vulnerable population all rely on signals from hormones in very narrow windows. Chemical highjacking of these systems at a young age can render permanent physiological damage that carries into adulthood. Children also do not have as robust immune systems, DNA repair mechanisms, blood-brain barriers, or detoxifying enzymes as adults to combat exposure to toxic chemicals, leaving them increasingly susceptible to adverse health effects.

Executive Summarv: Grub Infestation/Response, Cheverus High School Athletics Fields
After: 1) years of strict compliance with the Landcare Management Advisory Committee applicable ordinances that require organic management practices (with respect to the application of fertilizers, pesticides, and weed control), 2) increasing our staff investment to 1.5 positions to
provide proper mowing, grooming, and watering, and 3) engaging a professional firm (Sports Fields of Monmouth, ME) experienced in organic land management practices with many school clients across the State, we reached a critical life-safety event this past fall that places our
student athletes, coaches, officials, and student athletes of visiting schools at significant risk of injury due to grub infestation of the playing field within Boulos Stadium, 267 Ocean Avenue.
The conclusion of our engaged (Sports Fields) and other consulted professionals specializing in the turf management care industry was that the grub infestation was severe, not being mitigated
by the use of organic methods, and had compromised over 20%+ of the playing surface of the
stadium filed due to not only the infestation, but the additional, collateral damage caused by birds and animals feeding off of the grubs and causing extensive damage.
After nearly having to move a home soccer playoff game to an alternate site due to safety concerns, we filed a Landcare Ordinance Waiver Application on December 3, 2024, complete with photos of grubs, their eggs, turf damage created by the grubs a11d their natural predators, and live video of a failed tensile strength test conducted by Sports Fields. The test measures the ability of grass turf to not tear away under the stress of footwear applied by student athletes
during competition.
The Application seeks to apply Acelepryn, a pesticide known to be successful to mitigate grubs
by a licensed professional applicator (Sports Fields) during the last two weeks of May which is
believed to be the best window of time to be successful against the infestation per the opinion of the professionals we have consulted. The pesticide has been deemed on its approved label as not
harmful to humans. Missing the May application window will mean missing the opportunity to
mitigate the grubs due to their life span patterns and contributing environmental variables and risking more extensive field damage.
After the next scheduled meeting of the Landcare Management Advisory Committee on Tuesday, February ll, 2025, to review and hopefully approve this specific matter, we hope to have the matter reviewed and approved at the City Council's Sustainability and Transportation Committee on February 12, 2025, and then approved at the City Council on March 3, 2025.

wl1o are residents of the City of Portland in addition to the city residents enrolled at both Deering
and Portland High School who visit our campus to participate in the sports of football, soccer,
lacrosse, and track.

Testimony of Sarah Woodbury, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, Defend Our Health In Support of LD 25, "An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund Wastewater Treatment Facility Planning and Construction of Infrastructure Projects." Before the Joint
Committee on Appropriations and Financial Affairs April 9, 2025
Senator Rotundo, Representative Gattine and Members of the Appropriations and Financial Affairs Committee. My name is Sarah Woodbury. I am the Vice President of Policy and Advocacy for Defend Our Health. Defend Our Health's mission is to make sure that everyone has equal access to safe food and drinking water, healthy homes, and products that are toxicfree and climate-friendly. I am here to testify in support of LD 25, "An Act to Authorize a General Fund Bond Issue to Fund Wastewater Treatment Facility Planning and Construction of Infrastructure Projects."
Maine is dealing with a real waste issue. Due to the necessary ban on the land application of biosolids, or sludge, to protect Maine's vital farmland, our state-owned landfill, Juniper Ridge Landfill (JRL), will eventually run out of space to manage the sludge. The sludge also requires materials added to it to protect the integrity of the landfill. While we have space currently, we need to prepare for the future instead of waiting until the last minute to manage this waste crisis. LD 25 will provide much needed resources to the state to help fund necessary upgrades and facilities to manage this issue.
LD 25 will help fund already proven technology such as allowing wastewater treatment plants to install technology such as sludge dryers and digesters. These types of systems can greatly reduce the volume of sludge to be disposed. They also make disposal easier as you're now dealing with a dry product instead of a wet product so you will also need less of other bulky materials for stabilization. Additionally, the less liquid you have, the less leachate you have that will end up being discharged into rivers, streams, and oceans as wastewater effluent, limiting further PFAS contamination to our vital waterways. The funds can also be used to support new technology and pilot programs that can help invest in better ways to manage sludge down the road.
The bottom line is that we need to invest in our wastewater systems. These are systems we all use and all benefit from. Every single legislator in this building has constiuents that depend on these systems to keep their communities and the environment safe. This is not an issue we can hope will get better over time without an influx of resources. The time to act is now, before we run into a real crisis that will force us to spend even more money to fix, putting pressure on local taxpayers. LD 25 is necessary for the continued success of our PFAS management, our landfill management, and our waste stream management. I urge this committee to support passage of LD 25 and vote unanimously "ought to pass".

Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Environment and Natural Resources Committee. My name is Stephanie Durrant, and I live in Cumberland, Maine. I am here to testify in support of LD 1177, "Resolve, Establishing a 3-year Moratorium on the Installation or Reinstallation of Synthetic Turf and Requiring a Study of the Public Health and Environmental Risks of Synthetic Turf".
I am originally from Seattle, and moved to Maine four years ago for my husband's job at Maine Med. I immediately fell in love with Maine's appreciation for living in harmony with natural spaces, a stark contrast from the overdeveloped metro I grew up in. The humidity, not so muchbut I digress. I know Mainers realize how unique this place is; the connection with the land and water is really special. I am testifying in support of this bill today, because before we blanket the state with plastic fields, I'm asking the committee to pause installations long enough to study the impact of synthetic turf on the environment we value, and the public health we must protect.
I have worn a lot of hats in my life that lead to my hesitation around synthetic turf, but the one I'm here to highlight today is being a mom. As a scientist, I could give you a litany of reasons why we should stem the tide of plastic turf fields- the documented environmental harms and health concerns are numerous. But MY top three reasons are my three children.
It's the best and the worst to be a kid. On the one hand, it can be a carefree time full of imagination, dirt and neighborhood games of capture the flag; on the other hand, so many things are out of your control. Decisions are made for you, around you, above you - and all of them impact YOU. As a kid you put a lot of trust in the adults who make these choices, mostly because you have to.
...You have to trust Decision Makers will remember that your small frame is more impacted by heavy metals and toxins of all kinds than full grown bodies are, and will work to keep your environment free from these harms.
... You have to trust that they remember there are critical windows of development for children when endocrine disruptors at any level - found in plastics, plastic grass included- can impact your development and future health.
.... You have to trust that Decision Makers remember when microplastics enter the environment, they also enter and accumulate in our bodies; we are not separate from our environments.
... You have to trust they remember your small body can't regulate heat as well, and plastic fields reach unsafe temperatures quickly- and that injuries from these unnatural surfaces are motivating professional athletes to move back to grass fields themselves.
Our kids face an onslaught of health harms every day, from their built spaces to the unregulated chemicals in their shampoo. As a parent, I can only do so much to protect them on my own. I'm asking the committee to pause new installation and reinstallation of synthetic turf to ensure we

are not adding to the toxic load of our environment and families. Progress does not need to equal plastic. Please carefully consider the options before momentum brings us to a place much harder to reverse than prevent. I admire Maine's ability to be authentic, and true to itself. I'm asking the committee to pause the parade of plastic grass to ensure we do not unintentionally harm what we value- the health of our families and Maine's natural and wild spaces. As a mom, I know our kids not only deserve it, they are depending on it. Thank you.

Environmental & Natural Resources Committee
Testimony of Zach Lemelin - Athletic Director, Sanford School Department Against LD1177
Resolve, Establishing a 3-year Moratorium on the Installation or Reinstallation of Synthetic Turf and Requiring a Study of the Public Health and Environmental Risks of
Synthetic Turf
Dear members of the Environmental & Natural Resources Committee, I appreciate the time given to address the committee. As the athletic director for the Sanford School Department, I am fortunate enough to work in one of the best school districts in our great state. Sanford High School has a population of nearly 1,100 students, with almost 50% participating in athletics at the high school level. Sanford Middle School is equivalent to SHS in terms of population and participation, which is something we are extremely proud of as a community and want to continue to protect and increase opportunities and participation when possible, because as we know, the more our youth are engaged, the higher levels of success they reach in all aspects of life.
Sanford is a hardworking community that is proud of the opportunities we can provide for our students. In particular, the state-of-the-art high school that was completed and opened in 2018. A major part of this project, which was funded by local tax dollars, is our turf field at Alumni Stadium. Our community knew this would be an asset, as we only had grass facilities in the past. Having a turf field allows our student-athletes to compete in one of the best facilities in the state. Alumni Stadium is a facility that is sought out multiple times a year for regional and state championship contests in soccer, field hockey, and boys & girls lacrosse from the Maine Principals Association. At the community level, our facility is used to help host the Sanford Soccer Association's annual Pete Levasseur tournament, which has more than 150 teams competing in the youth soccer tournament, along with multiple youth football games in this venue each year. All of these events take place in conjunction with the 85-plus games in the fall and spring, and practices 6 days a week to accommodate the high school teams. Simply put, if Alumni Stadium did not have a turf field, we would not have the ability to host these events, which would be demoralizing for our community.
The wear & tear on a grass field from daily sports practices and multiple games a week would make our fields unsuitable and potentially unsafe due to the seasonal weather conditions we experience in our state. As a community, we take great pride in the opportunities and experiences that we can offer our youth and young adults, and the decision to install a turf field was not something we took lightly.
Our community and the previous athletic director spent countless hours researching and developing a plan to answer any questions that might arise as to whether or not turf fields are

unsafe. It was determined that, while there are risks associated with nearly every decision we make in life, the opportunities a turf field presents would outweigh any of the risks for our community in supporting our student-athletes.
Proposing a ban on synthetic turf will create an issue across our community and state, and in my opinion, cost the taxpayers more money in maintenance and care that most schools/communities cannot afford or find the knowledgeable and trained individuals to provide maintenance on grass fields. This bill would create a higher chance for unsafe playing fields, missed opportunities for skill development, and a lack of championship-caliber venues for the youth and high school student-athletes across this state. As an educator, athletic director, and parent, I want to help provide the best opportunities for our students and children when it comes to community-based sports and education-based athletics in the State of Maine, and this bill would be counterintuitive to that process.
I once again thank the committee for your consideration, and I respectfully ask for your opposition to LD 1177
Sincerely,
Zach Lemelin Athletic Director Sanford School Department
